प्रदूषण से जुड़े आंकड़ों और हवा में मौजूद जहरीले तत्वों को मापने और सार्वजनिक करने की सरकारी व्यवस्था की विश्वसनीयता पर सवाल उठा दिया है. शोधकर्ताओं, पत्रकारों और पर्यावरण एवं जनस्वास्थ्य से जुड़े कार्यकर्ताओं ने सबसे ज्यादा चिंता वायु गुणवत्ता सूचकांक (एक्यूआई) के आंकड़ों के गायब होने को लेकर जताई. खासतौर पर पीएम2.5 और पीएम10 जैसे सबसे ज्यादा प्रदूषण फैलाने वाले सूक्ष्म कणों के स्तर का डाटा उपलब्ध नहीं था. दिवाली की रात कई घंटों तक केंद्रीय प्रदूषण नियंत्रण बोर्ड (सीपीसीबी) के कई मॉनिटरिंग स्टेशनों पर इन प्रदूषकों के आंकड़े नहीं दिखे. जबकि इसी दौरान दूसरे प्लेटफॉर्म और दिल्ली प्रदूषण नियंत्रण समिति (डीपीसीसी) के मॉनिटरिंग स्टेशनों ने प्रदूषण का बेहद गंभीर स्तर दर्ज किया. दरअसल, दिवाली की रात दिल्ली के सीपीसीबी के कुल 59 मॉनिटरिंग स्टेशनों में से 45 पर किसी न किसी समय कम से कम एक प्रदूषक का प्रति घंटे का डाटा उपलब्ध नहीं था. वहीं, इसी अवधि में डीपीसीसी के मॉनिटरिंग स्टेशनों पर प्रदूषण का स्तर सामान्य सीमा से 60 गुना तक दर्ज किया गया. इसका असर अगले दिन सरकार की ओर से जारी वायु गुणवत्ता के आंकड़ों की विश्वसनीयता पर भी पड़ा. सरकारी आंकड़ों में औसत एक्यूआई वास्तविक स्तर से कम दर्ज किया गया. सेंटर फॉर रिसर्च ऑन एनर्जी एंड क्लीन एयर (सीआरईए) के विश्लेषक मनोज कुमार ने सोशल मीडिया प्लेटफॉर्म एक्स पर लिखा, “8 नवंबर की आधी रात से 9 नवंबर की सुबह 5 बजे तक दिल्ली के सीपीसीबी के 59 मॉनिटरिंग स्टेशनों पर पीएम2.5 के प्रति घंटे के 227 रीडिंग गायब थीं. केवल 14 स्टेशनों ने पूरा डाटा दर्ज किया, जबकि बाकी 45 स्टेशनों पर कम से कम एक घंटे की रीडिंग उपलब्ध नहीं थी.” उन्होंने आगे कहा, “चिंता की एक बड़ी वजह यह है कि कई रीडिंग उस समय गायब हुईं, जब प्रदूषण का स्तर मॉनिटरिंग उपकरणों की अधिकतम माप सीमा यानी 1,000 माइक्रोग्राम प्रति घन मीटर (µg/m³) के करीब पहुंच रहा था. ऐसी रीडिंग को प्रति घंटे या पूरे दिन का औसत निकालने और एक्यूआई तय करने के दौरान महज गायब आंकड़े मानकर नजरअंदाज नहीं किया जाना चाहिए. ऐसा करने से प्रदूषण का वास्तविक स्तर कम आंका जा सकता है.” पर्यावरण विशेषज्ञ और गैर-लाभकारी संस्था आईफॉरेस्ट के सीईओ चंद्र भूषण के मुताबिक, दिवाली के अगले दिन केंद्रीय प्रदूषण नियंत्रण items.title: CPCB has an explanation for missing Diwali data. It doesn’t have a solution
items.summary: Delhi-NCR’s Diwali was its most polluted in five years and, by official data, the fourth most polluted day of the year. But once again, it exposed gaps in pollution data and the government’s system to measure and publicise air toxicity. What created concern among researchers, journalists and environment and public health activists was the missing AQI data , particularly levels of the most polluting PM2.5 and PM10 particles. Many Central Pollution Control Board monitoring stations did not even show these numbers for several hours while other platforms and Delhi Pollution Control Committee’s monitors recorded severe toxicity. In fact, as many as 45 of Delhi’s 59 CPCB monitoring stations lacked hourly data for at least one pollutant at some point of time during Diwali night. For the same period, DPCC stations showed pollution levels as high as 60 times the normal limit. This impacted the credibility of the air pollution data released by the government the following day, as the average AQI was recorded lower than its actual value. Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) , wrote on X : “From midnight on 8 November until 5 am on 9 November, 227 hourly PM 2.5 observations were missing across 59 CPCB monitoring stations in Delhi. Only 14 stations reported complete data, while the remaining 45 had at least one missing hourly observation.” He said, “A key concern is that many missing readings occurred when concentrations approached the monitoring instruments’ upper measurement limit of 1,000 µg/m³ (micrograms per cubic meter). These observations should not simply be treated as missing when calculating hourly or daily averages or deriving AQI. Doing so could underestimate pollution levels.” According to Chandra Bhushan, an environmental expert and CEO of non profit organisation iForest , the CPCB should have explicitly disclosed, the day after Diwali, that data from several monitoring stations had not been included in the 24-hour average. Sunil Dahiya, founder of Envirocatalysts , said, “We have seen in the past too whenever the pollution levels approach 1000 microgram per cubic metre, the data from some CPCB monitoring stations go missing.” The CPCB however, issued a two-page official clarification on this matter, making several points. items.title: Delhi High Court seeks explanation from magistrate for six-month delay in pronouncing order
items.summary: The Delhi High Court has sought an explanation from a Judicial Magistrate First Class (JMIC) for a delay of over six months in pronouncing an order on an application seeking vacation of stay in a case [ Pradeep Bansal & Ors Vs State NCT of Delhi and Anr ]. Justice Manmeet Pritam Singh Arora also sought an explanation from the Chief Judicial Magistrate and the District Judge, regarding the context in which the JMIC made the remark that “this Court is working with only one stenographer and has a pendency of more than 4,500 cases.” The Court noted that similar remarks appeared in subsequent orders passed by the concerned judicial officer. Justice Manmeet Pritam Singh Arora The Court passed the order in a petition filed by one Pradeep Bansal and others for expeditious disposal of their application for vacation of an interim stay order passed by the Judicial Magistrate First Class (Mahila Court) in December 2023. The counsel representing the petitioners said the arguments on the application were heard on January 6 this year and that the matter has remained pending for the pronouncement of the order since April 22. The Court said it was unable to discern any reason for the non-pronouncement of the order from the trial court's order sheets. Therefore, the High Court directed the registry to seek a report from the trial court. The matter will be heard next on December 3. Advocates Nitesh Mehra, Kunal Raj, Hitaakshi Mehra and Riya Jain appeared for the petitioners. Standing counsel Rahul Tyagi and advocate Sangeet Sibou appeared for the State. [Read Order]

items.title: From lectern to bench: Why law professors belong in India’s higher judiciary
items.summary: Teaching law is a lifelong apprenticeship and that is the premise of this blog: law professors, who live inside legal developments every day deserve a real place among those considered for the higher judiciary. The framers of our Constitution agreed. Article 124(3)(c) makes a citizen eligible for the Supreme Court if he or she is, in the opinion of the President, "a distinguished jurist". Yet, in more than 76 years, not a single jurist has entered the Court through this door. The High Courts have no such door at all, since Article 217(2) admits only those with 10 years of judicial office or 10 years at the Bar. The silence has now been broken from within the Court itself. On August 30, 2026, addressing the LL.M. convocation of National Law University, Delhi, Justice Ujjal Bhuyan called the clause one of the Constitution’s "unused mandates" . He dismissed the objection that scholars lack courtroom experience as shallow, pointing to academics who serve on constitutional courts in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and Kenya. So, does the world’s experience support the lectern-to-bench route, or warn against it? The record of professor-judges across the globe is richer and more mixed than either side of the debate usually admits. Why professors make strong judges Currency of knowledge: A professor cannot teach last year’s law. Every new statute - such as the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 that replaced the Indian Penal Code - and every landmark ruling must be read, digested and explained to a room of skeptical students. Classroom questions work as a constant stress test of what the teacher knows. Systemic thinking: A judge decides the dispute in front of the court; a scholar studies how thousands of such disputes fit together. The professor brings the habit of asking whether a ruling is coherent with the wider body of doctrine and what it will mean for the next hundred cases. Comparative and theoretical depth: Questions of privacy, proportionality and sentencing increasingly turn on comparative reasoning and legal theory. Academics read foreign courts and jurisprudence as routine work, not as an occasional luxury. Judgments that teach: Scholar-judges tend to write structured and reasoned opinions. items.title: NCLAT rejects appeals by Yes Bank co-founder Rana Kapoor’s wife against insolvency of four firms
items.summary: The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) recently dismissed four appeals filed by Yes Bank co-founder Rana Kapoor’s wife Bindu Kapoor against the initiation of insolvency proceedings against four companies where she was a director before suspension [Bindu Kapoor Vs Mamta Binani] A bench of Officiating Chairperson Justice Yogesh Khanna and Technical Members Barun Mitra and Ajai Das Mehrotra upheld the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), New Delhi’s April 7 order admitting insolvency petitions against Imagine Estate Private Limited, Imagine Home Private Limited, Imagine Residence Private Limited and Imagine Habitat Private Limited. “The impugned order suffers from no illegality and thus all above appeals are dismissed,” the NCLAT held in its November 6 judgment. The insolvency petitions were filed by JC Flowers Asset Reconstruction Private Limited, which had acquired the lender’s rights under the loan and security documents. The principal dispute concerned whether the four companies had merely provided assets as security for a ₹105 crore loan extended to Bliss House Private Limited or had also undertaken obligations as corporate guarantors. This distinction determined whether the NCLT at New Delhi could hear the petitions despite the companies having their registered offices in Mumbai. Kapoor argued that the companies were only hypothecators and had not executed corporate guarantees. She maintained that the insolvency petitions should have been filed in Mumbai. However, Section 60(2) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) requires proceedings against a corporate guarantor to be brought before the NCLT where insolvency or liquidation proceedings against the principal corporate debtor are pending. Bliss House was already undergoing insolvency proceedings before the NCLT, New Delhi. Its admission into insolvency has been upheld up to the Supreme Court, the appellate tribunal recorded. Taking Imagine Estate’s case as the lead matter, the NCLAT examined the loan agreement and hypothecation deed together.
